evidence_notes: No source-reviewed cases support redirect-following as the shared mechanism. Cases like bigsk1, cbioportal, DHIS2, FastGPT, and mcp-atlassian should not be counted as redirect-following positives without source evidence showing an initial allowed URL followed by an unsafe redirected destination.
The representative_cases field is empty, meaning no case-level evidence links this guideline to actual vulnerability instances.

The guideline description itself is well-formed and could be retained as a candidate mechanism, but it needs at least one source-reviewed case where redirect-following is the confirmed boundary before it can be accepted.
main_issue: The guideline text is internally coherent as a standalone vulnerability mechanism (source shape, sink, missing guard, exploit precondition, and safe fix all align around redirect-following SSRF), but the source-reviewed evidence does not establish redirect-following as the shared boundary for any of the cases in this group. The representative_cases list is empty, and the rationale explicitly states that gl_mech_0116 examples mostly establish direct URL/proxy SSRF, renderer external-resource SSRF, or credential/trust-boundary confusion—not redirect-following.

evidence_notes: DHIS2 CVE-2022-41949: source evidence confirms SVG → Batik PNGTranscoder.transcode without KEY_ALLOW_EXTERNAL_RESOURCES=false; fix adds the flag. Strong evidence of content-triggered external resource resolution.

XWiki CVE-2026-42140: source evidence confirms PlantUML server URL from macro parameters → renderDiagram without trusted-domain validation; fix parses URL and checks URLSecurityManager.isDomainTrusted. Strong evidence of render-service destination SSRF.

Both cases have committed source evidence that directly supports the mechanism boundary. The exploit precondition (attacker supplies content/parameters → renderer initiates network requests) is satisfied in both cases.
main_issue: The two cases represent two sub-flavors of renderer-based SSRF (content-triggered external resource resolution in DHIS2/Batik vs. render-service destination SSRF in XWiki/PlantUML), but the core mechanism—rich-content input reaches a renderer/transcoder that initiates network requests without an enforced external-resource policy—is coherent and the boundary text covers both sub-flavors adequately. The missing_guard field already acknowledges renderer-specific variations. Keeping them together as a single mechanism is justified because both are renderer-path SSRF, distinct from direct HTTP proxy or redirect-following SSRF.
mechanism_name: renderer or document converter external-resource SSRF

evidence_notes: bigsk1__openai-realtime-ui::CVE-2026-5803: direct source-snapshot evidence shows req.query.url → fetch(fullUrl) without URL parsing or address policy. Strong evidence.
cbioportal__cbioportal::CVE-2024-41668: direct source-snapshot evidence shows path-info → RestTemplate.exchange() without scheme/host/private-address policy. Strong evidence.

labring__fastgpt::CVE-2026-44284: evidence is from committed r8 worklist records, not direct source snapshots. Mechanism fit is confirmed (MCPClient URL → StreamableHTTPClientTransport/SSEClientTransport without internal-address gate), but evidence should be source-expanded with direct snapshot references before final release.

sooperset__mcp-atlassian::CVE-2026-27826: committed r5/r8 group evidence shows header-provided URLs → JiraConfig/JiraFetcher and ConfluenceConfig/ConfluenceFetcher without destination validation. Also overlaps credential-forwarding risk which may warrant a separate audit dimension.

All four cases converge on the same missing-guard shape: the destination is not parsed and validated before the request, no private/metadata address ranges are rejected post-DNS, and no allowlist constrains scheme/host/port. The safe-fix semantics (parse→validate→reject internal→validate redirects→request) are consistent across cases.
main_issue: The boundary correctly captures the shared source→sink→missing-guard pattern across all four cases. Each case shows attacker-influenced destination material (query param, path info, header, config) flowing into a server-side network client (fetch, RestTemplate, MCP transport, fetcher) without destination validation. The rewrite from redirect-following to direct URL/proxy is justified: redirect following is a guard variant, not the mechanism itself, and the old framing overfits the group name while losing the shared source/sink/guard shape.
mechanism_name: direct SSRF through attacker-controlled outbound URL fetch
suggested_guideline: Direct URL/proxy SSRF: attacker-controlled request parameters, path components, headers, tool configuration, or equivalent request metadata are used to construct an outbound HTTP, proxy, MCP, webhook, or REST-client destination, and the server performs the request before enforcing scheme, host, port, DNS-resolved address, private-network, metadata-address, and redirect-target policy on the same destination object.
